title.ko: 1강. 보다 와 처럼: 두 가지 비교
title.en: Lesson 1. 보다 vs. 처럼: Two Ways to Compare

blocks.md:
In English, we use words like *“than”* and *“like / as”* to make comparisons. In Korean, two key particles handle these comparisons, but they operate in completely different ways:

1. **보다 (“Than...”) — Degree Comparison**:
   - Compares **measure, speed, size, or quality** along a scale (*more / less*).
   - Often paired with **더** (*more*):
     - *“비행기가 기차**보다** 더 빨라요.”* *(Airplanes are faster than trains.)*
     - *“형이 저**보다** 키가 커요.”* *(My older brother is taller than me.)*
     - *“어제**보다** 오늘이 더 따뜻해요.”* *(Today is warmer than yesterday.)*

2. **처럼 (“Like / As...”) — Similitude & Manner Comparison**:
   - Compares **resemblance, appearance, or manner** (*like an angel, like a Korean speaker*).
   - Very similar in meaning to **같이** (*like*):
     - *“천사**처럼** 착해요.”* *(Kind like an angel.)*
     - *“한국 사람**처럼** 한국어를 잘해요.”* *(Speaks Korean like a Korean person.)*

**The Classic Learner Mistake: Swapping 보다 and 처럼!**

- Saying *“저**처럼** 키가 커요”* means *“He is tall **like me**”* (both of us are tall, sharing the trait).
- Saying *“저**보다** 키가 커요”* means *“He is taller **than me**”* (comparing height on a scale).

Whenever you are saying something is **more / less than** something else, always choose **보다**!

items.tip: Airplanes are faster than trains. (Degree: 보다)
Today is warmer than yesterday. (Time degree)

blocks.q: You want to compare temperatures: "Today is colder than yesterday." Which sentence is correct?
blocks.why: Comparing degrees on a scale (colder than yesterday) requires 보다: 어제보다 더 추워요. 처럼 means "like/as", not "than".

blocks.q: You want to praise a friend’s fluency: "You speak Korean like a Korean person." Which particle fits best?
blocks.why: Comparing resemblance or manner ("like a Korean person") takes 처럼: 한국 사람처럼.

blocks.q: What is the difference between "형보다 커요" and "형처럼 커요"?
options: 형보다 커요 means taller than older brother; 형처럼 커요 means tall like older brother
형보다 커요 means shorter; 형처럼 커요 means taller
형보다 커요 is polite honorific; 형처럼 커요 is casual banmal
형보다 커요 is past tense; 형처럼 커요 is future tense
blocks.why: -보다 expresses degree ("taller than"), while -처럼 expresses resemblance in appearance or manner ("tall like").

blocks.meaning: Trains are much faster than buses.
blocks.why: Comparing speeds on a scale (faster than) takes 보다.

blocks.hint: When comparing degree with "더" (taller than me), use 보다 instead of 처럼: 저보다.

title.en: Lesson 2. 부터 ~ 까지: Start to Finish

blocks.md:
When speaking about schedules, working hours, travel routes, or study plans, you need to mark the **start** and the **end** of a range.

That’s where the dynamic duo **부터** and **까지** come in!

1. **부터 (“From... / Starting from”)**:
   - Marks the starting point in time, sequence, or number.
   - *“아침 9시**부터** 일해요.”* *(I work starting from 9 AM.)*
   - *“1페이지**부터** 읽으세요.”* *(Please read starting from page 1.)*

2. **까지 (“Until / To / By”)**:
   - Marks the ending boundary in time, space, or sequence.
   - *“오후 6시**까지** 일해요.”* *(I work until 6 PM.)*
   - *“서울에서 부산**까지** 기차로 가요.”* *(I go from Seoul to Busan by train.)*

3. **Paired Together: [A]부터 [B]까지 (“From A to B”)**:
   - *“월요일**부터** 금요일**까지** 출근해요.”* *(I go to work from Monday to Friday.)*

**Standalone 까지 as a Deadline (“By...”)**

When **까지** is used alone with a future time, it frequently expresses a **strict deadline**:

- *“내일**까지** 숙제를 내세요.”* *(Submit homework **by tomorrow**.)*
- *“5시**까지** 사무실로 오세요.”* *(Please come to the office **by 5 PM**.)*

Both **부터** and **까지** attach directly to nouns with **no batchim changes**!

items.tip: I work from Monday to Friday. (Time range)
Please send the document by tomorrow. (Deadline)
Lunch hour is from 12 to 1. (Everyday schedule)

blocks.q: Your office working hours are 9:00 AM to 6:00 PM. How do you describe this daily schedule in Korean?
blocks.why: 부터 marks the starting point (9시부터) and 까지 marks the ending point (6시까지): 9시부터 6시까지 일해요.

blocks.q: Your teacher sets a deadline: "Please submit your homework by tomorrow." Which sentence is correct?
blocks.why: 까지 indicates a deadline ("by a certain time"): 내일까지 숙제를 내세요. (내일부터 means starting tomorrow).

blocks.q: Which particle pair correctly completes the sentence: "도서관은 아침 9시(__) 저녁 10시(__) 열어요."?
blocks.why: Start to end time range takes 부터 (from) and 까지 (to): 9시부터 10시까지.
The ending boundary of a time interval takes 까지: 12시부터 1시까지.

blocks.q: Put in order: "I commute to work from Monday to Friday."
Match each expression with its role in a sentence:

blocks.hint: Place the starting time first with 부터, followed by the ending time with 까지: 9시부터 6시까지.
blocks.why: Range starts with 부터 and ends with 까지: 9시부터 6시까지 일해요.

title.ko: 3강. 만 과 밖에: "오직" 두 가지 방법
title.en: Lesson 3. 만 vs. 밖에: Two Ways to Say "Only"

blocks.md:
Both **만** and **밖에** translate to *“only / just / nothing but”* in English, but they are **the single biggest grammatical trap for Korean learners**!

Master this one core rule, and you will never make this mistake again:

1. **만 (Neutral “Only / Just”) — AFFIRMATIVE & NEGATIVE**:
   - Works freely anywhere! You can use it with **both positive and negative verbs**:
     - *“물**만** 마셔요.”* *(I only drink water. — Affirmative)*
     - *“사과**만** 안 먹었어요.”* *(Only the apple was not eaten. — Negative)*
     - *“지갑에 천 원**만** 있어요.”* *(I have only 1,000 won.)*

2. **밖에 (Restricted “Nothing but / Only”) — STRICTLY NEGATIVE ONLY!**:
   - **밖에 literally means “outside of / other than”**.
   - Therefore, it **MUST ALWAYS be followed by a negative predicate (없다, 안, 못, 모르다)**!
     - *“지갑에 천 원**밖에 없어요**.”* *(Outside of 1,000 won, I have nothing = I only have 1,000 won.)*
     - *“사과**밖에 안 먹었어요**.”* *(I ate nothing except apples.)*
     - *“한국어는 인사말**밖에 몰라요**.”* *(I know nothing of Korean other than greetings.)*

**🚨 FATAL GRAMMAR ERROR: Never use 밖에 with an affirmative verb!**

- ❌ *천 원밖에 있어요.* (**IMPOSSIBLE IN KOREAN!**)
- ❌ *사과밖에 먹었어요.* (**IMPOSSIBLE IN KOREAN!**)

If the ending verb is affirmative (*있어요, 먹었어요, 알아요*), you **MUST USE 만**:
- *천 원**만** 있어요.* (O)
- *사과**만** 먹었어요.* (O)

If the ending verb is negative (*없어요, 안 먹었어요, 몰라요*), you can use **밖에** to emphasize scarcity:
- *천 원**밖에** 없어요.* (O)

items.tip: I have only 1,000 won left. (밖에 + 없어요: Negative)
I have only 5 minutes. (만 + 있어요: Affirmative)
I drank nothing but water. (밖에 + 안 마셨어요: Negative)

blocks.q: Which sentence contains an IMPOSSIBLE grammatical error in Korean?
blocks.why: 밖에 can NEVER be paired with an affirmative verb like 있어요! It must always be followed by negative verbs like 없어요: 천 원밖에 없어요.

blocks.q: You want to say: "I only drank water today." The verb is positive (마셨어요). Which particle MUST you use?
blocks.why: Positive affirmative verbs cannot take 밖에. You must use 만: 물만 마셨어요. (To use 밖에, the verb must be negative: 물밖에 안 마셨어요).

blocks.q: Complete the sentence expressing that you have very little money left: "지금 지갑에 오백 원(__) 없어요."
blocks.why: Coupled with the negative verb 없어요, 밖에 emphasizes that there is nothing other than 500 won: 오백 원밖에 없어요.

blocks.sentence: 기차가 떠날 때까지 시간이 5분[밖에] 안 남았어요.
blocks.meaning: There are only 5 minutes left until the train departs.
blocks.why: Paired with the negative 안 남았어요 to express scarcity, use 밖에.

blocks.q: Put in order: "I currently have only 1,000 won on hand."
Match each sentence with its grammatical characteristic:

blocks.wrong: 초급 최다 실수: 회의 전까지 시간이 5분밖에 있어요.
blocks.hint: 밖에 can never take positive 있어요! Change to negative 없어요 (5분밖에 없어요) or use 만 (5분만 있어요).
blocks.why: 밖에 requires negative verbs: 시간이 5분밖에 없어요 (or 시간이 5분만 있어요).

blocks.wrong: 긍정문 오류: 오늘 아침에 사과밖에 먹었어요.
blocks.hint: Affirmative verbs (먹었어요) take 만: 사과만 먹었어요 (or 사과밖에 안 먹었어요).
blocks.why: Positive 먹었어요 takes 만: 사과만 먹었어요.

blocks.q: Negative limit: "I have only 1,000 won in my wallet."
blocks.hint: 지갑에 + 천 원밖에 없어요 / 천 원만 있어요

title.ko: 4강. 실전 비교: 견주기와 범위(보다 · 처럼 · 밖에) 총정리
title.en: Lesson 4. Summary & Practice: Comparison & Scope Particles

blocks.md:
In this course, you learned three powerful particles that compare things or set strict limits:

1. **-보다 (Comparison - Than)**: Attached to the standard of comparison.
   - 비행기가 기차**보다** 빨라요. *(Airplanes are faster than trains.)*

2. **-처럼 / -같이 (Simile - Like/As)**: Attached to something you resemble or do alike.
   - 영화배우**처럼** 멋있어요. *(Cool like a movie actor.)*

3. **-밖에 (Exclusive Limit - Nothing But)**: MUST be followed by a negative predicate (`없어요`, `몰라요`, `안 먹어요`).
   - 지갑에 천 원**밖에 없어요**. *(I have nothing but 1,000 won.)*

rows: Attach to what is being compared against

items.tip: Today the weather is much warmer than yesterday. (어제보다 than yesterday)
The teacher is warm-hearted like an angel. (천사처럼 like an angel)

items.ch: 아침에 바빠서 사과 반 개밖에 못 먹었어요.
items.tip: I was busy in the morning, so I could only eat half an apple. (반 개밖에 못 먹었어요)

blocks.q: Which sentence correctly uses the comparison particle -보다 to say "Korean is more fun than English"?
blocks.why: To compare against English ("than English"), attach -보다 to 영어: 영어보다 더 재미있어요.

blocks.sentence: 동생은 가수[처럼] 노래를 정말 감미롭게 잘 불러요.
blocks.meaning: My younger sibling sings really sweetly like a singer.
blocks.why: To express similarity ("like a singer"), attach -처럼 (or -같이) to 가수: 가수처럼.

blocks.q: 밖에 is strictly paired with negative verbs: 「시간이 5분 ___ 없어요. (There is only 5 minutes left.)」
blocks.why: With a negative verb like 없어요, use 밖에 to mean 'nothing but / only': 5분밖에 없어요.

blocks.q: Grammar check: Which sentence has a critical error with -밖에?
blocks.why: 밖에 can NEVER be used with positive 있어요! It must be used with a negative verb: 천 원밖에 없어요 (or with 만: 천 원만 있어요).
